ety.text: Originated 1542, from Classical Latin cynicus (“Cynic/cynic”, adjective) + -al. By surface analysis, cynic + -al. In reference to dogs, with allusion to the ultimate etymology (Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós, “doglike”)).

senses.d: Of or relating to the belief that human actions are motivated only or primarily by base desires or selfishness.
ex: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received.

senses.d: Skeptical of the integrity, sincerity, or motives of others.
Bitterly or jadedly distrustful or contemptuous; mocking.
Showing contempt for accepted moral standards by one's actions.
Like the actions of a snarling dog, especially in reference to facial nerve paralysis.
ex: Demetrius Attalicus studied the symptomatologies due to strictura cerebri, characterized by a cynical spasm of the facial nerve.

grp.label: of or relating to the belief that human actions are motivated by base desires or selfishness

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin cynicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós).
Borrowed from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós), probably from the name of the Cynosarges, a public gymnasium in Athens where Antisthenes taught.
From the past participle of resabiar.
